articles.title: Google Signals A Wider Crackdown On UGC SEO Spam via @sejournal, @martinibuster
articles.fullContent:
Google takes aim at a new source of SEO spam, signaling that platforms, tools, and services may face consequences for content published by their users. It’s also a warning to SEOs and website owners who leverage these kinds of sites for links and AI search influence.

Adds sharing platforms as a type of site that can be penalized for UGC spam.

Provides steps that platforms can take to prevent UGC Spam

Advises on how to become aware of harmful activities and manual actions

All three advisories are specific to platforms which means that Google may take actions against these kinds of sites. SEOs who are promoting sites with these kinds of sites should become aware of these policies and the platform owners should also be aware of these new guidelines.

Change 1: Spam Advisory Addresses Sharing Services

The first change is the addition of a few words that add these sharing platforms as the kinds of sites that the guidelines apply to.

These are the new words added to the page:

“…and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps…”

This is the full context, with the newly added words in italics:

“Spammers often take advantage of open comment forms and other user generated content inputs and generate spammy content on an unsuspecting victim site. Hosting platforms and tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps may be similarly open to abuse; spammers may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies and add little or no value to the web.”

Google may be planning to target tool and app platforms that enable users to generate content. SEOs should add this to their site audits to check if clients are using these kinds of sites in manipulative ways. Platform owners should take notice and make necessary changes as outlined in the next sections.

Google may in the near future crack down on tool and app platforms that enable users to generate content on the web pages of those platforms.

The second change to the spam support page explains what platform owners should do in order to prevent harmful behavior on their platforms that could result in a manual action by Google (removal from the search results).

Google added an entirely new section that is targeted at platforms or websites that allow user generated content. The new guidelines outline steps the platforms should take to avoid receiving a manual action.

These steps are specific to platforms that enable users to generate web pages. This also includes services that are meant for content sharing or collaboration.

The new section advises users of these kinds of sites and platforms to use the no-index directive on pages that are not meant to be indexed by search engines. For example, use a no-index rule in either the robots.txt or with a meta no-index tag if the function of a service is to generate shareable pages or tools but are not meant to be indexed.

“Only index content meant for Search If your service lets users create shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools, consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or only accessed directly by people with a link.

When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default.”

The third and last change to Google’s spam page is an explanation of how to track and recognize the signs that users are causing potentially negative changes to a a website and how to know when a site has reached a point where Google has taken action against it.

This is the new section added to the website:

“Verify your site or subdomain in Search Console so you receive email alerts if Google issues a manual action against your site or detects security issues. Also check the Page Indexing report and Search performance report regularly for unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries that don’t match your platform’s purpose.

Track platform-level creation and indexing metrics, and set up alerts for anomalies such as spikes in newly published public pages or a small number of users generating a large share of indexable URLs.”

Google Expands Its UGC Spam Guidelines Google’s updated policies now explicitly address platforms that enable users to publish shared pages, AI-generated content, and web apps, extending the guidance beyond traditional user-generated content.

Platforms Face Greater Responsibility For User-Generated Spam Google’s changes put platform owners on notice that allowing users to publish spam can expose the entire platform to search penalties.

Google Draws A Distinction Between Shareable Content And Indexable Content Not everything users create is intended for search engines. Google advises platforms to prevent indexing of content intended primarily for sharing, collaboration, or utility.

Spam Prevention Becomes A Platform-Level Responsibility Google’s updated guidance emphasizes proactive prevention, monitoring, and early detection of abusive publishing activity rather than waiting for a manual action.

Implications For SEO Audits SEOs should consider whether clients use third-party publishing platforms in ways that violate Google’s spam policies and whether the platforms themselves are vulnerable to abuse.

Potential For Expanded Enforcement The changes suggest Google may be paying closer attention to spam originating from platforms that enable users to publish generated content, although the updated guidance does not establish that a crackdown is imminent.

Google updated its user-generated spam guidelines to explicitly address platforms that enable users to publish shared pages, generated content, and web apps, putting platform owners on notice that they may face search penalties for spam published by their users. The changes suggest Google is taking a closer look at how these platforms are being abused and may be preparing for greater enforcement.

articles.title: Social media leadership skills for 2026 (+ KPIs to track)
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media leadership skills combine strategic thinking, emotional intelligence, AI fluency, and cross-functional communication to guide enterprise teams toward business outcomes.
  2. The biggest shift in 2026 is leading AI adoption responsibly, balancing speed and governance without losing the human element.
  3. Strong social leaders measure success through team health, brand reputation, and business impact, not vanity metrics.
  4. Developing social media leadership skills requires structured feedback, clear decision-making frameworks, and a willingness to experiment and fail fast.

What are social media leadership skills?

Social media leadership skills are a blend of abilities, both learned and innate, that help leaders direct and inspire social media teams to succeed. They matter at every scale, but they matter most in enterprise environments where one decision can ripple across dozens of markets.

The core skills include:

  • Strategic thinking: Connecting social activity to business goals like revenue, retention, and reputation, rather than treating channels as standalone projects.
  • Emotional intelligence: Reading the room internally and externally, spotting burnout early, and handling sensitive moments without defensiveness.
  • Communication aptitude: Explaining social performance in language the C-suite, legal, and frontline teams all understand.
  • AI fluency: Knowing which tasks to hand to AI, which to keep human, and how to govern the output.
  • Adaptability: Shifting plans quickly when platforms, policies, or culture change without losing the thread of the strategy.
  • Creativity and innovative thinking: Creating room for teams to test new formats, including the ones that look strange on a slide.
  • Collaboration and conflict management: Navigating competing stakeholder priorities and saying no when the request does not serve the strategy.

A successful social media leader’s skills must go beyond social media management. A true leader understands how to delegate and guide in real time through an evolving industry and culture. They know how to use a social strategy to achieve business goals.

It’s no surprise, then, that a recent IBM study found 69% of CEO respondents say their organization’s success is directly tied to maintaining a broad group of leaders with a deep understanding of strategy and the authority to make critical decisions. Social is no exception.

Shakivla Todd, a 4-time Shorty award-winning Social Media Strategist, says a great social leader must be “naturally culturally aware and in-the-know.”

“You don’t need to be chronically online. But you do need to be acutely aware of what’s happening as it pertains to current events and cultural moments.”

Cultural relevance isn’t just to stay ‘on trend,’ says Todd. It’s to “help lead your team through culturally sensitive moments. An exceptional social media leader should know how to read the damn room, everyone hates a tone-deaf brand.”

In short: social media leadership skills are the mix of strategic, human, and technical abilities that turn a capable social team into a business function executives rely on.

How is social media leadership different from management?

Social media leadership sets the direction; social media management executes against it. Both roles are essential, and most leaders have done both, but the day-to-day work looks very different.

Social media managers focus on executing a social media strategy. Their social tasks include:

  • Creating and publishing compelling content
  • Understanding how social networks like LinkedIn, TikTok, or Instagram work
  • Engaging an audience
  • Analyzing and optimizing performance
  • Maintaining brand voice

Social media leaders, on the other hand, set a direction and keep everyone working toward it. They:

  • Shape the long-term vision
  • Advocate for resources
  • Build systems that allow their teams to move quickly while staying aligned

A manager might be optimizing a campaign’s engagement rate. A leader is the one asking how that engagement ladders up to revenue, reputation, and retention.

In social, business leaders have to stay flexible. The industry changes fast, and you need to be able to pivot, using new trends and real data, to build initiatives that actually move the business forward.

“Keeping up with the swiftness of social media is an Olympic sport,” says Todd. “I’ve learned to be comfortable with uncertainty, and I don’t get too attached to plans.”

What does a social media director do?

A social media director sits between management and leadership, owning the strategic direction of social while staying close enough to the work to guide it. The role is usually where social media leadership skills get tested for the first time at scale.

Typical social media director responsibilities include:

  • Strategy ownership: Setting the annual social strategy and making sure every channel maps to a business objective.
  • Team oversight: Hiring, structuring, and developing the social team, including agency and freelance partners.
  • Budget and resourcing: Building the business case for headcount, tools, and paid support.
  • Executive reporting: Translating social performance into the metrics leadership already tracks.

articles.fullContent:
By Jenny Rooney AI gives every marketer access to similar tools. So, how’s that going to help your brand stand out?

Live from the Marketing Vanguard stage at Brandweek 2026 , Jenny Rooney sits down with Mastercard’s EVP of global brand strategy and innovation, Cheryl Guerin, to talk about how brands can differentiate themselves when technology becomes table stakes.

Cheryl gets into how Mastercard uses AI to eliminate routine brand work and free its people for higher-order thinking, why Priceless has survived nearly three decades of cultural change, and why real agility sometimes looks like saying no.

How Mastercard uses automation to free brand experts for higher-order creative work

Why Priceless has remained relevant across nearly three decades of cultural change

Why saying no is becoming a critical part of brand agility

How “passions experts” help Mastercard identify cultural opportunities earlier

Why emerging talent can create different economics and stronger relationships than obvious superstar bets

Why purpose-driven work has to connect brand ethos, constituent needs and business impact

This episode is part of a special vidcast series that was recorded live during Brandweek 2026 and presented in partnership with Tatari.

Cheryl Guerin has spent nearly 26 years at Mastercard across a wide range of roles, including regional marketing leadership, products and services, P&L responsibility and global credit before returning to the area she describes as her heart: marketing.

Over that time, Cheryl has helped evolve the Priceless platform through major shifts in culture, technology and the business itself, leading initiatives such as the True Name card and Touch Card. Her perspective is grounded in a simple challenge: keep the brand relevant as the world changes without losing the human truth that made it matter in the first place.

[02:03] AI Cannot Differentiate Your Brand — Cheryl’s Brandweek 2026 AI take cuts straight through the hype. If everyone eventually has access to similar technology, the tool itself cannot become the advantage. Mastercard is already using AI to absorb routine brand questions, with its brand assistant handling roughly 75% of work that used to be answered manually. But the win is not simply efficiency. It is giving experienced brand people more time to think about harder questions around creativity, trust and the future of the brand.

[04:16] Why Priceless Still Works Nearly 30 Years Later — Mastercard has had to flex Priceless through culture shifts, technology shifts and major changes in the business. What has not changed is the human idea underneath it. Cheryl traces the platform back to a move away from material signs of success toward intangible experiences. Nearly three decades later, she points to Gen Z’s desire for belonging and in-person experiences as evidence that the underlying truth has become more relevant, not less.

[10:07] What Is Still Worth an Agency Premium? — Mastercard’s relationship with McCann has lasted nearly as long as Priceless itself. Cheryl sees that creative partnership as essential, but she is equally clear that not every piece of work needs premium agency resources. As daily content, B2B marketing and full-funnel execution increase, Mastercard has expanded its own internal capabilities. The split is increasingly deliberate: keep agencies close to the big creative thinking, while building internal muscle for the volume and speed modern marketing demands.

[13:27] Why MasterCard Hires “Passions Experts” — Mastercard does not rely only on generalist marketers to understand music, sports, esports or motorsports. Cheryl describes specialists who deeply understand those communities and know how to connect cultural knowledge back to business outcomes. That expertise helps the brand identify talent before everyone else does, balance globally recognizable names like Lady Gaga with emerging bets and compete without necessarily being the biggest spender in the category.

By Adweek Staff What makes a fashion brand feel authentic, build lasting loyalty, and create campaigns that genuinely move culture? It starts with understanding people, not chasing trends.

In this episode of Adspeak by ADWEEK, host Lauren Finney Harden brings together three global fashion marketing leaders: Anne Cambria of Sephora, Elizabeth Money of Béis, and Fabiola Torres of Gap.

Recorded live at Brandweek 2026 , the conversation explores how democratized style, emotional storytelling, and data-informed creativity are reshaping the way brands connect with consumers.

The discussion examines why brands must give communities a voice in shaping trends, how authentic relationships can turn campaigns into cultural moments, and why human stories often resonate more deeply than polished brand messaging.

The guests also share how marketers can balance creative instinct with data, build meaningful customer connections in an AI-driven world, and use real-world experiences to strengthen brand loyalty.

For brands working with limited budgets, the conversation offers a valuable reminder: understanding your audience, delivering quality products, and staying true to your identity can be more powerful than chasing the next viral moment.

Why democratization of style means brands must let communities vote on trends, not dictate them

How to engineer virality through emotional storytelling

The “Data as Guardrails” Framework for blending gut instinct with analytics

How to humanize a brand by putting employees, founders, and real customer stories front and center

Why analog and in-person experiences still build stronger loyalty

How small and challenger brands can compete without big budgets

Fabiola Torres is the Global CMO at Gap and is known for her expertise in building emotional brand connections through creative campaigns. With a background in bridging generational gaps through music, fashion, and style, she has spearheaded viral campaigns like the Cat’s Eye collaboration that drove unprecedented engagement and business growth.

Elizabeth Money is the SVP of Brand & Creative at Béis, bringing over 20 years of experience in the travel and fashion industries. Known for her human-centered approach to brand building, she has transformed Béis from a DTC startup into a community-driven lifestyle brand by prioritizing authentic consumer connections over data-driven metrics. She also offers practical advice for challenger brands seeking to build genuine loyalty and market presence.

Anne Cambria is SVP of Brand, Retail, and Creative Marketing at Sephora, and she specializes in empowering self-expression through beauty and retail innovation. With a focus on inclusivity and community amplification, she has helped establish Sephora as a diverse beauty authority by centering client voices and experiences.

Lauren Finney Harden is the moderator and a veteran marketing journalist, bringing editorial expertise to discussions on brand strategy and cultural trends. Her perspective bridges the traditional publishing world with modern marketing practices, offering a unique lens on how brands now function as editors themselves in shaping consumer culture and style.

articles.title: Consumers Hold the Mic: Fanta Gives Them Something to Talk About
articles.fullContent:
By Matt Britton For decades, marketers could afford to build a brand around one big piece of communication. Today, consumers move across retail, social, entertainment, search, physical experiences and, increasingly, AI-powered environments.

The challenge now is knowing what about the brand should stay fixed, and what needs to change with the culture around it.

In this episode of The Speed of Culture, Ibrahim Khan, global VP of marketing at Fanta, joins Matt Britton to unpack this dichotomy. From adapting occasions, and packaging across markets to building Fanta’s Haunted Universe for Halloween, Ibrahim explains why strong global brands protect their fundamentals while constantly reinventing how people experience them.

He also makes the case that marketers need to get over the “hangover of the TV era” and start treating the product, retail experience, live experience, and consumer conversation as part of one connected brand system.

Ibrahim Khan leads strategy for Fanta, a global beverage brand with $18 billion in retail value. His career spans nearly two decades across major consumer brands, including Coca-Cola, Sprite, and Fanta, with experience across Pakistan, Thailand, Southeast Asia, and global markets. His approach to marketing is grounded in one fundamental truth: Marketing still has to drive the business.

[00:54] Brand Truth Needs New Expression — Ibrahim argues that the fundamental reason people choose a product rarely changes dramatically from market to market. What does change is how people experience it: language, channels, daily routines, cultural habits, and consumption occasions. For a global marketer, consistency does not mean executing the same way everywhere. It means knowing which parts of the brand are non-negotiable, and giving local markets room to express them differently.

[03:54] Assumptions Are the Enemy of Global Marketing — Cultural relevance can materially change business strategy. Ibrahim points to beverage consumption with food as an example: that occasion is less developed in parts of Asia than in Western markets, leading Fanta to lean more heavily into leisure occasions there. Even visual conventions differ. An in-store environment that initially felt overwhelming to him turned out to match what consumers in that market expected. The marketer’s instinct to “simplify” is not automatically universal.

[08:07] Not Every Cultural Moment Needs Your Brand — Ibrahim is disciplined about cultural participation: “not every festivity needs a brand, and not every brand needs a festivity.” Fanta leans into Halloween because indulgence, fun, and soft-drink consumption already belong naturally within the occasion. His warning to marketers is equally clear. Chasing passion points or trends where the product has no authentic role can make the work feel forced instead of relevant.

[09:39] Build a Platform, Not Just Another Annual Campaign — Fanta has spent years building around Halloween, but Ibrahim says the ambition has now moved beyond year-to-year collaborations. Haunted Universe is designed as an expandable world of characters, stories, lore, partnerships, and experiences that can develop over many years. Fanta researched horror archetypes across cultures and fandoms before entering the space, treating entertainment IP as something to build deliberately rather than a seasonal advertising stunt.

[15:05] AI Can Scale the World Without Replacing Human Taste — Ibrahim sees technology as an enabler of bigger creative worlds, much as advances in animation and graphics changed entertainment before it. But he draws a firm distinction between capability and authorship. Marketing contains art, taste, ethics, and judgment that he still sees as inherently human. For Fanta’s Halloween work, AI supports an effort shaped by a large group of people rather than replacing the people doing the creative thinking.

[25:06] Marketing Needs to Get Over the TV Hangover — Twenty or thirty years ago, Ibrahim says, marketers could shape most brand perception around a 30-second TV commercial. He believes that success has made the industry lazy. Today, the product itself needs to become a marketing channel, and marketers need to think across the full offer rather than obsessing over communication alone. His sharpest point: consumers now hold the microphone. If they are not talking about what the brand is doing, the old tools cannot manufacture the same relevance they once could.

Matt Britton is America’s leading expert on the millennial generation having consulted for over half of the Fortune 500 over the past two decades. He is the Founder and CEO of Suzy and the host of The Speed of Culture Podcast.

articles.title: Instagram Reels for business in 2026: Best practices + examples
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Instagram Reels deliver higher reach and engagement than other Instagram post types, which makes them the most effective format for business visibility in 2026.
  2. The Reels algorithm prioritizes watch time and completion rate, plus shares and saves, so hooking viewers in the first 1-2 seconds matters most.
  3. Mixing trending formats with evergreen content like tutorials, behind-the-scenes clips, and product demos builds short-term reach and long-term audience growth.
  4. Scheduling Reels at optimal times and tracking performance metrics helps teams refine strategy and prove ROI.

What is an Instagram Reel?

An Instagram Reel is a short-form vertical video shared on Instagram. You can record, edit, and stitch multiple video clips and photos together, then add extras like:

  • Original audio or trending sounds
  • Voiceovers
  • Text overlays and stickers
  • Effects and transitions

Source: Starface

Bonus: Claim your pack of free animated Instagram Reels templates created by Hootsuite’s professional designers. Easily customize them in Canva, and take your Reels game to the next level today.

What’s the difference between a Reel and a TikTok?

Reels and TikToks are both short-form video platforms, but they differ in audience, reach, content style, and more.

Here’s a breakdown of the main differences between a Reel and a TikTok:

How long can Instagram Reels be?

Reels can be up to 3 minutes long. That change took effect in January 2025, raising the limit from the previous 90 seconds.

That said, just because you can post longer videos doesn’t mean you should. According to Adam Mosseri, Head of Instagram, when it comes to Reels, the shorter the better.

Check out his Reel below on the ideal Reel length:

Source: Adam Mosseri

What video sizes and specs work best for Instagram Reels?

The best Instagram Reels size is 1080 x 1920 pixels with a 9:16 aspect ratio. Because Reels are designed for full-screen mobile viewing, vertical videos perform best.

Here are the recommended Instagram Reels specs:

  • Aspect ratio: Between 1.91:1 and 9:16
  • Resolution: 1080 × 1920 pixels recommended (minimum 720p)
  • Frame rate: Minimum of 30 frames per second (FPS)

Why use Instagram Reels for business?

Instagram Reels are worth the investment because they reach people who don’t follow you yet across a platform where half of U.S. adults are active, which is hard to do with any other post type. Instagram has said that through its recommendations, creators of all sizes have an equal chance of breaking through and reaching new audiences, and Reels are the format that recommendation engine favors.

Here’s what that means for a business account:

  • Reach beyond your followers: Reels surface in the Reels feed and on Explore, so a single video can introduce your brand to people who have never heard of you.
  • Higher engagement: Reels tend to earn more interactions per post than static images or carousels, largely because saves, shares, and rewatches all count. Use an engagement rate calculator to benchmark yours.
  • Discoverability through search and audio: Search-friendly captions, on-screen text, and sounds all give Instagram more context to match your video with interested viewers.
  • Commerce built in: Product tagging lets viewers tap straight from a Reel to a product page, shortening the path from discovery to purchase.
  • Trust and authenticity: Faces, voices, and unpolished moments give audiences a sense of who’s behind the brand in a way a product photo can’t.

In short, Reels are the most efficient way to buy attention on Instagram without paying for it, which is why they belong in almost every brand’s social media strategy.

Key Takeaways

  • The 4 Ps (product, price, place, and promotion) are tools marketers use in combination to shape how a product (or range of products) is positioned, promoted, and sold to a specific group of customers. Together, they’re often referred to as the “marketing mix.”
  • The marketing mix is fundamentally a tech-agnostic framework for helping with important marketing decisions. 
  • “Product” looks at how well features meet needs, “price” at what customers are willing and able to pay, “place” at the best ways to distribute a product, and “promotion” at building market awareness. 
  • Well-known companies like Rolex, McDonald’s, and Red Bull have perfected the 4 Ps behind their products and brand identities.
  • AI is changing how marketers execute the 4 Ps, but the fundamental questions behind product, price, place, and promotion remain the same.

The 4 Ps of marketing (product, price, place, and promotion) have been around for decades, and they still drive decisions around every successful product launch.

Also known as the “marketing mix,” they help you think through how to bring a product to market and reach the customers most likely to buy it.

It doesn’t matter if you’re running a one-person small business or a global enterprise. The 4 Ps help you bring a product to market and get it in front of people most likely to buy it.

How you put the 4 Ps to work has changed, though. AI is giving marketers new ways to understand their customers and make more informed decisions, often in less time.

I’ll cover some of these opportunities as I show you how the 4 Ps still drive marketing decision-making today.

What Are the Four Elements of the Marketing Mix?

The 4 Ps of marketing, commonly known as the marketing mix, stand for product, place, price, and promotion. They’re like four levers companies can adjust to better position their products for the customers they want to reach.

Here’s the meaning behind each of the four Ps: 

  • Product: What you’re selling, including its features, packaging, and the support that comes with it
  • Price: What you charge and how you structure the pricing
  • Place: Where and how your customers can buy the product
  • Promotion: How you get the word out about the product

To more fully understand the 4 Ps of advertising, we need to take a step back. Mention “marketing,” and most people think of customer-facing content like ads, social media posts, emails, videos, and blog articles like this one. 

In fact, these represent just one piece of a much broader discipline. They’re the “promotion” part of the mix called marketing communications.

True marketing is a big-picture process that strives to meet all customer needs. And thinking in terms of the 4 Ps allows companies to do exactly that. 

What About the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs?

The idea of a marketing mix has been around longer than the 4 Ps themselves.

In 1948, Harvard professor James Culliton described marketing executives as “mixer(s) of ingredients.” Inspired by this idea, fellow Harvard professor Neil Borden often referred to the concept of the marketing mix in the years that followed. 

Then in 1960, marketing professor E. Jerome McCarthy organized it into the four elements we know today in his book Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach.

Other models have been suggested in the years since, with two in particular gaining traction: the 7 Ps and the 4 Cs:

  • The 7 Ps: In 1981, marketing professors Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner expanded the 4 Ps to better suit service-based businesses. Their model adds people, process, and physical evidence to the mix. These cover the employees who deliver a service, the delivery process, and the environment where business takes place. 
  • The 4 Cs: Marketing professor Robert Lauterborn proposed a more customer-oriented alternative to the 4 Ps in 1990. His model replaces them with consumer wants and needs, cost, convenience, and communication. Instead of starting with what a business wants to sell, the 4 Cs push marketers to focus on what customers actually need. 

These alternative models add some useful nuance. To me, though, the 4 Ps still make up the strongest foundation for marketing campaigns. What is a social media dashboard?

A social media dashboard is a single interface that pulls metrics from all your social accounts into one place for tracking, analyzing, and reporting on performance.

Enterprise marketing teams, agencies managing multiple clients, and growing social teams rely on them most, because the reporting burden scales with every new account and campaign.

Instead of logging into Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook, TikTok, and X separately to check results, a dashboard brings everything together. You get a single view of what’s working, what’s not, and how your social efforts connect to business goals.

Most dashboards include real-time or near-real-time data, customizable visualizations (charts, graphs, tables), and the ability to filter by platform, date range, campaign, or metric. They range from free tools like Google Looker Studio to connected systems like Hootsuite Social OS that combine scheduling, publishing, and cross-platform analytics in one place.

What are the four types of social media dashboards?

Dashboards tend to fall into four categories, and knowing which one you’re building keeps you from cramming every metric into a single view. The four types are operational, analytical, strategic, and tactical.

  • Operational: Day-to-day monitoring of live activity, like incoming messages, mentions, and publishing status.
  • Analytical: Deeper performance analysis across longer time ranges, used to find patterns in content, formats, and audiences.
  • Strategic: High-level KPIs and ROI reporting for leadership, usually reviewed monthly or quarterly.
  • Tactical: Campaign-specific tracking with a start and end date, focused on whether a single initiative hit its targets.

Most of the templates later in this article map to one of these four types, so you can match the template to the job you’re actually trying to do.

Why should you use a social media dashboard?

Dashboards solve a measurement problem that grows with your budget. With over $121 billion in US social ad spending projected for 2026, the cost of not knowing what’s working keeps rising. For enterprise teams managing multiple accounts, campaigns, and stakeholders, dashboards solve real operational problems.

Faster, easier reporting

Switching between native analytics on every platform to compile a monthly report can eat up hours. A dashboard lets you export all the data and visualizations you need for presentations and reports in minutes, not hours. That time goes back into strategy and execution.

Real-time decision-making

When performance data is scattered, you’re always reacting late. A dashboard gives you an at-a-glance view of what’s working (and what’s not), so you can pivot your social media strategy when it actually matters. AI-powered insights can surface trends and anomalies you might otherwise miss.

Proving social media ROI to leadership

One of the biggest challenges for social teams is connecting their work to business outcomes, especially when 59% of CMOs report insufficient budget to execute their strategy. Budget conversations go better when you can show the trend line, not just last month’s numbers, particularly with marketing budgets flat at 7.8% of revenue.

articles.title: How to build your social media team for the future of marketing
articles.fullContent:
It’s certainly not 2010 anymore. So why are so many businesses still resourcing social media teams as if it is?

Social teams have evolved far beyond publishing posts and responding to comments. Today, they manage content and video production, influencer partnerships, customer care, social search, paid media, community engagement and increasingly, social intelligence. Social’s role is expanding across the business, and a social team’s structure needs to evolve with it.

Organizations are also looking to social data for more than marketing insights. According to Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report, 93% of leaders view social intelligence as essential for future growth, yet only 10% of organizations have embedded it into enterprise strategy. Closing that gap requires more support for social teams that are already stretched across a growing list of responsibilities. They need the right people, roles and processes to turn social data into action across the business while creating more capacity for strategic work.

There’s no one-size-fits-all social media team structure. But the strongest teams connect their work directly to business outcomes rather than organizing solely around the tasks they complete. Building for that future requires the right mix of specialized expertise, cross-functional relationships and technology to keep pace with social’s expanding role.

In this guide, we’ll break down how to structure a social media team, which roles to prioritize and how to build and manage a team that’s prepared for the future of marketing.

How to structure a social media team

Social’s dynamic nature can give marketers a professional advantage if leaders give them space to grow. With the right structure, teams can quickly refine and grow their skills, creating career-making opportunities.

Proactively experimenting with new social media department structures can also shift a brand’s trajectory—helping it win a larger audience, build customer loyalty and sustain growth.

Here are four common models to consider, plus how your structure may evolve as your company grows.

1. Functional

The functional model organizes social media team roles around specific responsibilities, such as influencer partnerships, social media intelligence or paid media. Generalists may also have defined focus areas, including content creation, video production and social search optimization (SOSEO).

At Sprout, the social team also partners closely with Brand Creative on asset development and with teams across the organization—including PR, Content, Customer Marketing, Events, Internal Comms, Revenue Marketing and Product Marketing—on messaging, research and distribution.

Constantly switching between incoming DMs, reporting, influencer coordination and content production can limit time for creative and strategic thinking. A functional structure can help reduce burnout, clarify ownership and create more room for social marketers to deepen their expertise.

With clearer focus areas, teams can scale priority initiatives and measure their impact more effectively. This model works especially well for organizations that want to support career development while assigning clear ownership to specific social priorities.

2. Network

Some teams align individual employees to specific networks, such as TikTok, Instagram, Facebook or LinkedIn. With this approach, each person owns a network strategy from development through execution, which in turn enables them to build deep network expertise.

Sprout’s social team experimented with a network-specific structure in 2022 before eventually moving away from it. While the model supported highly intentional content and stronger network-specific audience insights, it wasn’t scalable for a growing team.

The social landscape has also become more fluid since network-based structures first gained popularity. New networks emerge and consumer preferences change rapidly, creating gaps or redundancies when roles are tied too closely to individual networks.

A network-based social structure can still work as an interim model for lean teams developing their social media marketing strategy from the ground up. As the team grows, shifting toward functional ownership can make it easier to adapt across networks.

3. Audience engagement

Another common team structure organizes social media team roles around audience engagement goals and customer needs. These typically fall into three categories:

  • Awareness: Creating content to increase brand visibility among new and existing audiences.
  • Engagement: Creating content and responding to comments, DMs and other inbound interactions to build community and strengthen brand loyalty.
  • Customer Service: Managing customer questions, requests and complaints to resolve issues quickly.

These teams often include specialists beyond content and community management. For example, an awareness-focused team might include a content creator, an influencer marketing strategist and a performance analyst who work together to develop relevant and effective content.

Because this model requires employees to work across multiple networks, centralized social media management software becomes especially important. Bringing publishing, engagement, reporting and collaboration into one system reduces time spent switching between disconnected platforms.

4. Center of excellence

In a social media center of excellence (CoE) model, representatives from different departments form a central council that shapes social strategy and establishes shared standards.

Participants may include leaders from PR, employer brand, HR, product, customer care and other teams that rely on or contribute to social. Together, they align priorities, improve information sharing and create clearer governance around how the organization uses social.

CoE models tend to work best for large organizations with social stakeholders spread across multiple departments or regions. A centralized group reduces silos and gives distributed teams a shared framework for decision-making, measurement and execution.

5. Structure by company size

Company size can help determine which structure makes the most sense, but complexity is often the better signal. A lean team may work well with broad ownership until the volume of channels, stakeholders and social data becomes difficult for a few people to manage.

As demand grows, teams usually need more specialization and clearer ownership. Enterprise organizations also need stronger governance, especially when social intelligence spans multiple departments. Key takeaways

  1. The most important employee advocacy metrics tie directly to business outcomes: reach, engagement, leads, hires, and ad spend saved.
  2. Calculating employee advocacy ROI means assigning dollar values to revenue, recruiting savings, paid media savings, and retention savings, then comparing that total against program costs.
  3. Benchmarking your results against your own historical data (and against mature programs) helps you spot what’s working and what needs fixing.

What does it mean to measure employee advocacy success?

Measuring employee advocacy success means evaluating your program’s business impact through key performance indicators (KPIs). A complete measurement approach tracks:

  • Reach and brand visibility: How far employee posts extend your brand beyond corporate channels
  • Engagement: Whether audiences are interacting with employee-shared content
  • Employee participation: How many employees are actively sharing, and how often
  • Business impact: This includes leads, conversions, hires, and ad spend saved

Tracking results turns fluffy numbers into evidence you can take to leadership. And with the right data, you can sharpen your strategy into a repeatable advocacy machine.

Real-world example: Victoria Samways, Marketing & Brand Manager at Major Tom, used employee advocacy measurement to prove a three-figure ROI on a single campaign.

  • The approach: Samways paired employee advocacy software with UTM tracking codes, then encouraged employees to share campaign content.
  • The result: Advocacy landed in Major Tom’s top 5 traffic sources for the campaign, generated over $100k in pipeline, and delivered a higher-than-average win rate.

Why is it important to measure employee advocacy success?

Measurement matters because advocacy programs compete for budget, attention, and headcount like every other initiative. Without data, they almost always lose that competition.

Here are three specific risks of running an unmeasured employee advocacy program:

  1. You can’t defend your budget. Measurement shows how your program moves the needle on reach, leads, and recruiting.
  2. You can’t fix what’s broken. Without data, you don’t know if low participation is a content problem, a platform problem, or a culture problem.
  3. You can’t replicate what’s working. Measurement shows you which campaigns, content types, and brand advocates are driving the strongest results. When you know what’s working, you can streamline your efforts and scale the wins.

There’s another upside that’s easy to underestimate: measurement makes employees take the program more seriously. And with 2026 social trends pointing to ROI as the defining factor of ambassador programs, that rigor has never been more important.

When employee advocates can see their own impact, they participate more and stick with the program longer. In other words, the act of measuring is itself a participation lever.

The bottom line: A social media post that racks up a thousand likes feels great, but if those likes aren’t turning into top talent, qualified leads, or customers, what’s the point? Measurement is what makes the impact of employee advocacy visible.

You build an employee advocacy measurement framework by deciding what the program is meant to achieve, then choosing the employee advocacy KPIs that map to each goal. Doing this first saves you from drowning in metrics that nobody in the business cares about.

Here’s a simple four-step framework to work through before you track a single share:

  3. Set your baselines: Record where each metric sits before the program launches (or before your next big push). Without a baseline, you have numbers but no story.
  4. Agree on a reporting cadence: Review participation and engagement monthly so you can course-correct quickly. Save business impact metrics like pipeline and earned media value for quarterly reviews.

Social media in healthcare is the use of public social platforms by healthcare organizations to communicate with patients, educate the public, recruit staff, and build their brand. articles.fullContent:
What is an employee advocacy program?

An employee advocacy program is a structured initiative that encourages employees to share company-approved content on their personal social media accounts to extend brand reach and build trust.

It’s a powerful part of any social media marketing and content strategy. Instead of relying only on your brand’s accounts to do the talking, employees post about your company on platforms like LinkedIn, X, or wherever they’re already active.

Sometimes that content is promotional, like a new campaign, product launch, or company milestone. Other times it’s cultural, offering a peek into what it’s actually like to work at your company.

The reason it works is simple: people trust other people more than they trust corporations. In fact, 88% of consumers say trusting a brand is an important or critical purchase criterion, on par with quality and value, according to Edelman.

When your employees share authentic stories, it humanizes your brand, boosts your organic reach, and helps you connect with your target audience in ways standard corporate messaging just can’t.

Successful employee advocacy programs are built on:

  • Clear marketing goals
  • Measurable KPIs to track performance
  • Easy-to-share content and guidelines for employees

The benefits for the company are wide-reaching:

  • Increased brand awareness,
  • Improved reputation,
  • Boosted engagement, and
  • Talent recruitment, to name a few.

In short, every employee share strengthens both your internal company culture and your external trust, turning your team into your most credible marketing channel.

Download a free employee advocacy toolkit that shows you how to plan, launch, and grow a successful employee advocacy program for your organization.

Download now

Informal advocacy vs. structured programs: what’s the difference?

The difference between informal advocacy and a structured program comes down to intention.

  • Informal advocacy: Spontaneous and personal. Genuine, but unpredictable. You can’t count on it, measure it, or repeat it.
  • Structured programs: Intentional, consistent, and built to scale, because employees get the tools, content, and guidelines they need to share regularly.

Most successful employee advocacy programs include:

  • Curated content hubs: Where employees can access pre-approved content
  • Training and resources: To help staff build their personal brand while staying on-message
  • Incentives or recognition: That encourage ongoing participation
  • Measurement and analytics: To track reach, engagement, and business impact

A platform like Parliament, the employee advocacy app inside Hootsuite Social OS, makes this simple. Employees get a curated feed of pre-approved content they can post in a few taps, while admins measure performance across every share, gamify participation with leaderboards, and keep posts aligned with brand and legal guidelines.

Summary: Informal advocacy is spontaneous and personal. Structured programs are intentional and strategic.

Why do companies invest in employee advocacy programs?

Companies invest in employee advocacy programs because they drive real business outcomes: wider reach, stronger reputation, better recruitment, and more pipeline, all at a fraction of the cost of traditional marketing.

To understand what this looks like in practice, we chatted with Victoria Samways, Marketing & Brand Manager at Major Tom, and a long-time user of Hootsuite’s employee advocacy tools.

“Our employees are very powerful brand ambassadors,” says Samways. “Each employee can easily have hundreds of connections on LinkedIn alone. Multiply that by the number of employees a brand has, and that’s a large audience.“

Here are the top employee advocacy benefits:

  1. Expanded brand reach and awareness
  2. Stronger talent attraction and recruiting
  3. Improved brand reputation and trust
  4. Higher organic engagement
  5. Sales pipeline and lead generation
  6. Career and personal brand benefits for employees

1. Expanded brand reach and awareness

Collectively, employees have a wide social reach. Tapping into your employees’ networks is one of the easiest ways to reach new audiences without spending a dollar on paid media. And it also feels more authentic.

The math is straightforward. A company of 500 employees with 500 LinkedIn connections each has access to a potential audience of 250,000 people, most of whom will never follow the brand page. That’s why brand reach is usually the first metric advocacy programs move.

2. Stronger talent attraction and recruiting

A careers page can promise great culture all day long, but a real employee sharing what it’s actually like to work there? That’s way more convincing.

When teams post authentically about their work (wins, projects, team moments, or even just what a typical day looks like), it offers a genuine peek at the employee experience.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Websites remain an important way for consumers to verify that a business is legitimate.
  • Wix’s State of Websites report found that search still accounts for 42% of website traffic.
  • Sites with structured data that passes Google’s rich-results inspection earn 2x more revenue and 9x more traffic than sites without it.
  • Blogs and reviews can strengthen a brand’s authority and contribute to business growth.
  • As AI changes discovery, a credible website can give consumers and AI systems a reliable source of information about a brand.

AI has made it easier than ever to create a website, generate content, and put a brand online. That speed comes with a new challenge: consumers have more reason to question what they see.

A convincing business can appear online almost overnight. For customers, a website therefore has an important job beyond selling products or services. It can help establish that a business is real.

Wix’s first State of Websites report, based on data from more than 300 million users, examines how websites are being built, discovered, and used in the age of AI. The report found that websites remain central to business growth, even as discovery expands across AI platforms and other channels.

For marketers, the takeaway is straightforward. Website credibility still matters. The challenge is making sure a website provides the information, content, and technical signals that support trust with both people and machines.

Why Websites Still Matter in the Age of AI

AI search is changing how people find information, but it hasn’t eliminated the need for a destination where customers can verify what they’ve learned.

Source

Websites Help Consumers Verify a Business

Wix’s research describes a growing tension around AI and website creation. Building a site is becoming faster, but customers still need confidence that a business is legitimate.

A consumer might discover a company through an AI recommendation, social platform, or traditional search result. Before making a purchase or contacting the business, they may visit its website to confirm that the company exists and learn more about what it offers.

That makes a website part of the validation process.

A professional domain, clear business information, useful content, customer reviews, and evidence of expertise can all contribute to website trust. These signals help answer a basic question that becomes increasingly important as AI-generated information becomes easier to produce: Is this business real?

AI Search Is Changing Discovery, Not Replacing Websites

The Wix report found that AI platforms are increasingly interacting with websites. Its data shows that LLMs still account for less than 1% of website traffic, although traffic from LLMs grew fourfold between 2024 and 2025.

Traditional search remains much more significant. Search accounts for 42% of traffic to Wix sites, compared with 40% from direct traffic and 13% from social.

This puts the current state of discovery into perspective. AI search is growing quickly, but traditional search continues to be a major source of website visits.

For brands, that means the website still needs to serve both audiences: people arriving directly or through search and AI systems looking for information to use in their responses.

What the Wix Data Says About Website Trust

The report highlights several website characteristics associated with stronger business performance.


Source

Structured Data Can Support Visibility

One of the clearest findings concerns structured data.

Wix found that sites with structured data markup that passed Google’s rich-results inspection earned 2x more revenue and received 9x more traffic than sites without it.

This is a correlation in Wix’s dataset, not evidence that adding structured data directly causes those outcomes. Still, the finding reinforces the importance of making website information easier for search engines and AI systems to understand.

Structured data gives machines additional context about the information presented on a page. As search experiences become more sophisticated, that machine-readable layer can help make important information easier to interpret.

For brands investing in AI visibility, technical foundations such as structured data should therefore remain part of the conversation.

articles.title: Building trust through social media: 5 ways to earn it
articles.fullContent:
Authenticity is the most important brand characteristic on social media, according to Sprout’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey. But as audiences grow more skeptical of what they see in their feeds, brands need to work harder to earn their trust.

People rely on social media for news, product recommendations and connection. At the same time, Sprout’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey found that 35% of users trust social media less than they did a year ago. AI-generated content adds to that skepticism, making it harder to distinguish real experiences from manufactured ones.

Sprout’s Be So FR webinar explored this “trust recession” and the growing demand for content that reflects real people and experiences. Brands need to show who’s behind their content and follow through when customers reach out.

Building trust through social media starts with what you publish and how you respond to your audience. In this guide, we’ll explore what earns audience trust and practical ways to strengthen it.

Why trust is now built on social media first

People often encounter your brand through someone else’s post before they visit your website. They search for recommendations, compare customer experiences and ask questions in the comments. Those interactions help them decide whether to trust you.

Sprout’s 2026 Pulse Surveys show how people use social to find information and decide what to buy:

  • Search: 21% of consumers turn to social media first when searching for information, according to Q2 data.
  • Influencer impact: 67% made a purchase directly because of an influencer’s recommendation in the past year.
  • Trends and culture: Q3 data found that 54% of consumers turn to social media to keep up with trends and cultural moments, ahead of TV and streaming at 45% and conversations with friends and family at 42%.

These social media statistics show why brands need to pay attention to conversations beyond their own accounts. With influencers playing such a significant role in what people buy, choosing credible partners matters.

For example, viewers of @theglownarrative’s skincare review discuss product prices, share what they want to try and recommend alternatives. Her review gives viewers a starting point, while the comments offer additional perspectives. Brands that partner with creators who share honest, firsthand experiences give potential customers more reason to trust their products.


The same online scrutiny applies when something goes wrong for a brand too. According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, consumers first hear about a brand crisis on social. And 64% say it’s important for brands to respond publicly on social rather than through a press release or website statement.

How building trust on social media is a growth lever

Social media’s influence gives brands a chance to turn audience trust into growth. When people trust your brand, they’re more likely to choose your products and recommend them to others. As Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey highlights, creating multiple points of connection with your brand and through partnerships with trusted voices can strengthen customer relationships and support growth:

  • Authentic influencer partnerships build buying confidence. Eighty-one percent of consumers say it matters whether an influencer has used the product they promote. Creators with firsthand product experience offer more credible recommendations.
  • Employee content introduces potential customers to your business. Forty percent of consumers rated employee-generated content as more authentic than posts from a brand’s main account. The same proportion discover products or services through employee content at least once a month.
  • Timely crisis responses protect customer relationships. Response speed influences how consumers judge a brand’s public crisis response. Addressing problems promptly and following through on a solution gives customers a reason to keep doing business with you.

The signals that earn audience trust

Building audience confidence starts with how your brand shows up day to day. The table below outlines four trust builders—consistency, responsiveness, transparency and proof—and the behaviors that undermine them.

You’ve heard it from mentors, recruiters and that coworker who posts on LinkedIn every morning: You need a personal brand. Truth is, you already have one, because people form a public perception of your brand whether you shape it or not. This guide shows you how to take control of that perception and turn it into real opportunities.

Personal branding once sounded like a celebrity-only game. Today, founders, marketers, job seekers and employees use it to stand out in crowded feeds and earn trust before they ever say hello. It’s how people decide whether to follow you, hire you or buy from you.

Branding yourself feels daunting when you don’t know where to start. But the strongest personal brands are built on who you already are.

You don’t need a massive following, a big budget or a magnetic personality. You need well-defined goals, a sharp sense of your value and the habit of showing up.

Ready to build yours? Let’s dig in.

What is personal branding?

Personal branding is how you present yourself as an individual to your audience. It’s the mix of expertise, values and personality people associate with your name. Our glossary definition covers the short version, and this guide shows you how to build one.

The idea isn’t new. Management writer Tom Peters popularized it in 1997 with his Fast Company essay “The Brand Called You.” Social media turned his idea into something anyone with a phone can act on.

Think about how corporate branding works. We associate specific feelings, values and expectations with brands we trust. Every company has a story and image.

The same applies to you and your personal brand. The difference comes down to who owns it, how it sounds and what it’s for.

People often treat personal branding as a synonym for being an influencer. It doesn’t have to be. A software engineer, a nurse and a small business owner can each build a personal brand without chasing fame.

Your brand should highlight your human side. Voices and personalities set brands (and people!) apart. Branding yourself means aligning your online persona with your real-life one.

Building your brand goes beyond just marketing yourself. Here are the key pieces of a personal brand:

  • Voice and values. That is, what you say and what you believe. Your brand voice shouldn’t be one-size-fits-all or robotic.

  • Content. What you create, and how you present it, attracts your audience. If you write long-form newsletters, mastering Substack SEO gets those deep dives discovered by new readers.

  • Creativity. You don’t need to be a creative genius to build a personal brand. But some sort of creative trademark helps you stand out from the crowd.

  • Personality. There’s no one-size-fits-all personality type for your brand. Energetic, laid back or suit-and-tie, you do you.

  • Authenticity. Your personal brand shouldn’t feel manufactured or made up. Align your online persona with who you are offline and your brand will never feel forced.

Why is personal branding important?

Here is why building a personal brand is worth the effort.

Standing out from the crowd

The people who’d benefit the most from a personal brand are often focused on building something else. A company, art, you name it.

Like it or not, everyone’s a content creator now. That means who we are and what we make are often one and the same.

Among the countless creators and marketers out there, growth is daunting. Your audience only has so much attention to give.

With a compelling brand and consistent content, you give yourself a chance to shine. People don’t grow audiences or garner influence by accident. And both your personal brand and what you create sit within your control.

Relatability and authenticity matter to modern audiences

According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, consumers rank authenticity and relatability as two of the three most important brand content traits. Apply the same logic to individuals. This matters even more in an era where “influence” can feel manufactured.

That’s your edge as an individual. Nobody else has your experiences, your opinions or your sense of humor.

Making stronger connections with your community

Your voice and values shape your ability to grow your audience. Putting your personality front and center attracts like-minded followers.

That also means engaging with your audience to understand their needs and challenges. This goes hand in hand with establishing trust and building meaningful relationships.

When followers feel seen, they comment, share and come back for more. That’s how an audience becomes a community.

Opening doors to career and business opportunities

A strong personal brand puts your expertise on display before anyone asks for it. Recruiters, clients, collaborators and event organizers find you, instead of the other way around.

What makes a strong personal brand?

A strong personal brand is specific, consistent and rooted in real value. Before you post anything, get well-defined answers to these questions.

  • Purpose: Why you’re building a brand at all (a new role, clients, a community or a product launch).

  • Niche: The narrow topic you want to be known for. Precision is memorable and breadth is forgettable.

  • Audience: The specific people you want to reach and the problems they need solved.

  • Value: What you give that audience that no one else does (expertise, perspective, entertainment or community).

  • Story: The experiences that explain why you care and why people should listen to you.

Reputation risk often shows up in small ways first. Customer concerns in one market, inconsistent messaging in another. Different teams respond to the same issue in different ways. Individually, they may seem minor. Together, they can reveal a much bigger problem.

Part of the challenge is how brands track reputation risk in the first place. Traditional approaches often focus on obvious changes after they happen, rather than connecting social and media signals that could point to an issue sooner. As a result, teams can miss early warning signs or struggle to piece them together quickly enough.

Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report found that most teams take one to two weeks to act on what they see on social, while only 10% respond within hours. This delay has real consequences. Eighty-six percent of organizations say siloed or slow-moving insights have caused them to miss opportunities, and 26% have seen customer issues escalate that could have been addressed earlier.

Atlas Copco Group, a global industrial company spanning air compression, vacuum, industrial and power technologies, wanted better visibility into those warning signs. Their approach shows what it looks like to move beyond monitoring and use reputation data more proactively. This article breaks down their process to show what a stronger reputation intelligence model looks like in practice.

What is reputation intelligence? (And why monitoring no longer cuts it)

Reputation intelligence connects brand data across markets, channels and social accounts so teams can spot patterns, understand them and decide what needs attention.

Reputation monitoring, on the other hand, focuses on tracking what’s already happening around your brand. It tracks signals like reviews, mentions and shifts in sentiment. Monitoring helps teams keep tabs on public perception, while reputation intelligence adds the context needed to make more proactive decisions.

For large organizations, that broader view turns scattered brand feedback into clearer guidance for communications, go-to-market strategies, governance and other business decisions. Teams can use the same reputation data to identify recurring issues and give leaders a better view of developing risks in the business.

Reputation risk hides in small signals, not big spikes

Many reputation management services focus on obvious changes, like a sudden spike in negative sentiment or a surge in brand mentions. By then, the issue is already visible enough to demand a response or have caused damage.

The first clues are usually less obvious. Maybe your customers start complaining about the same thing or more of their questions go unanswered. Engagement might drop or online conversations about your brand might take on a more negative tone.

When Atlas Copco Group’s team dug into how conversations about their brand actually evolved, they saw that many risks started as smaller patterns: repeated questions, inconsistent account activity, off-brand content, inactive pages, declining quality signals or fragmented local execution.

These signals are easy to miss when you rely on alerts alone because each one can seem too minor to warrant attention. With social intelligence, Atlas Copco Group brings those signals together to spot patterns that need a closer look before they impact business performance.

Atlas Copco Group’s 5-step reputation intelligence model

Atlas Copco Group manages social in multiple business areas, divisions and local markets. Operating at this scale means protecting brand trust and compliance while enabling local teams to respond quickly to their audiences.

The team addressed that challenge by shifting from reactive reputation management to a more proactive governance model, earning Atlas Copco Group Sprout’s 2026 Predictive Edge Award.

The model is based on five practices that help them spot emerging risk, strengthen brand presence and manage issues consistently.

1. Catch weak signals early

Atlas Copco Group tracks weak signals that could point to larger reputation issues. Recurring customer and internal team behavior patterns are all indicators that brand consistency or account health may be slipping. Tracking these patterns across markets helps the global team focus on the bigger picture and provide guidance so local teams can stay close to their audiences and market.

To identify which weak signals matter for your brand, start with the reputation risks you already monitor and work backward. What behaviors, questions or changes tend to show up before those risks become more serious? Those early indicators can become the signals your team tracks more closely.

Using Sprout Social Listening, the Atlas team tracks these patterns across channels and spots connections that might be easy to miss when looking at each account on its own. From there, the team can then investigate what’s happening and decide whether a local market needs more guidance.

2. Establish a clear governance framework

Early signals are more useful when teams know what to do with them. Atlas Copco Group created a social media action matrix that sets clear expectations around account ownership, daily content checks and account health scorecards published every six months.

Those shared expectations also strengthen brand safety. When multiple teams and contributors manage social accounts, clear ownership and review processes create more consistency around how teams publish content and respond to potential issues.

Atlas Copco Group uses Tagging in Sprout to organize content by quality and compliance, track which teams are meeting brand standards and identify where additional support is needed.

3. Standardize account health metrics

Atlas Copco Group uses a consistent set of metrics to evaluate brand health in various markets. The team looks at activity, brand compliance, response times and audience engagement together to create a more objective view of performance.

articles.title: Email Marketing in the AI Era: Personalization, Automation & Deliverability
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • AI adoption in email is concentrated in content production. Personalization, automation, and deliverability, where the bigger revenue gains sit, get far less attention.
  • Personalization is moving from broad segments, like geography and demographics, to individual, predictive targeting.
  • Automation’s share of email revenue grows with company size. Businesses over $51 million in revenue get 71 percent of email revenue from automation versus 11 percent from campaigns.
  • Nearly a fifth of sent emails never reach the inbox, and most of that loss happens before a subscriber has any chance to engage.
  • The programs that win connect personalization, automation, and deliverability into a single system that reinforces itself.

Have you noticed your team is sending more emails than ever, but the results don’t feel any different?

Most marketers are pointing AI at email marketing’s wrong problem. The real opportunity is understanding customer intent, automating decisions, and personalizing experiences at scale. Most teams are using AI to write more emails without fixing the parts of the program that actually drive revenue.

Email personalization, automation, and deliverability are the three areas that actually move that revenue. Inboxes are getting louder as AI makes content creation easier, and louder rarely means more relevant. The rest of this post walks through what’s changing in each area, and how to build them into one connected system.

The AI Shift: What’s Changing in Email Marketing

Marketing teams are under real pressure right now: do more with fewer resources, scale personalization, improve retention and lifetime value, and increase marketing efficiency, all at once. AI looks like the obvious answer.

The problem is where that AI effort is actually going. Ask marketers what their biggest email challenge is today, and list growth tops the list at 29 percent, followed by personalization at 25 percent. Deliverability comes in last, at just 6 percent, even though it’s the foundation everything else depends on. An email that never reaches the inbox can’t be personalized or well-timed enough to matter.

Source

The New Email Marketing Framework

Here’s how the pieces break down:

  1. Personalization: delivering the right message.
  2. Automation: delivering it at the right moment.
  3. Deliverability: making sure it reaches the inbox at all.

You can’t improve these levers in isolation and expect the same lift each time. A gain in one gets erased by a gap in another. Perfect personalization that lands in spam accomplishes nothing, and flawless deliverability paired with generic, one-size-fits-all messaging just means more people ignoring an email they did receive.

Personalization in the AI Era

Most brands are stuck in what amounts to a segmentation trap. They personalize using broad buckets, new versus returning customers, geography, industry, demographics, and call it personalization. Only 34 percent of companies actually use AI-driven or predictive email marketing personalization. Another 24 percent are still at basic audience segmentation, and 5 percent use no personalization at all.

Most teams have the customer data needed for real personalization, they just aren’t using it to predict what happens next. Teams rate themselves strongest in measurement and attribution, with 55 percent calling that capability strong or very advanced. They rate themselves weakest in customer data and identity, at just 37 percent strong or advanced, along with AI skills and governance.

Personalization moves through three stages. Demographic personalization (location, age, gender) is the easiest to set up but produces broad assumptions and low relevance. Behavioral personalization (products viewed, purchases, engagement) produces higher engagement and better conversion. Predictive personalization goes a step further, using purchase likelihood, churn risk, and lifetime value to guide what happens next.

Open rates already vary by age group, from roughly 20.6 percent among 18-24-year-olds up to 25.7 percent among 55-64-year-olds, which makes a strong case for layering behavioral and predictive signals on top of basic demographic segmentation.
