articles.title: Holiday shopping is happening earlier than ever, here’s what brands need to know
articles.fullContent:
Halloween candy is still on the shelves, but holiday shoppers are making wish lists and hunting for deals months before the holidays arrive.

But as the shopping season gets longer, budgets are getting tighter. For brands, that means more chances to get in front of consumers, but also more competition for every dollar shoppers spend.

Data from Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey points to three factors that will define the holiday season: campaign timing, price sensitivity and meeting shoppers where they’re increasingly discovering gifts—on social.

Consumers don’t want earlier holiday campaigns, except when they do

Consumers have mixed feelings about how early holiday marketing should start.

According to Sprout’s Q3 2026 pulse survey, nearly half (49%) say campaigns launched as early as August make them more likely to buy, including 19% who say they’re much more likely. Just 11% say an early start makes them less likely to purchase.

But ask consumers when brands should launch their holiday campaigns and the story changes. Half point to October or November as the ideal window, compared to 21% who prefer August or September. Another 12% say brands should wait until December.

Those findings may seem contradictory, but they point to a distinction between when consumers want holiday marketing to dominate their feeds and when they’re open to discovering seasonal products. Shoppers can be receptive to gift ideas, new products and seasonal inspiration well before they want brands to go all-in on holiday messaging. In other words, an earlier presence can influence what they eventually buy without making it feel like the holiday season starts in late summer.

The sweet spot: Show up early without going all-in. Use August and September to build awareness and consideration, then ramp up your holiday campaign in October and November.

For example:

  • Tease what’s coming: Preview holiday collections, seasonal launches or upcoming offers.
  • Get gift-worthy products on shoppers’ radar: Introduce products consumers might want to add to their lists before they’re ready to buy.
  • Start publishing seasonal content: Share gift inspiration and other useful holiday content that gives shoppers a reason to engage early.

Starting earlier gives you more room to test what resonates before peak shopping begins. Then you can put more support behind the products, messages and offers gaining traction.

Brands are already putting this approach into practice. Fenty Beauty, for example, launched its limited-edition holiday collection in September, giving shoppers an early look at its seasonal products. As of writing, the TikTok has received over 100K views and over 5K likes.

Timing also depends on who you’re trying to reach. Younger consumers are especially receptive to an early start: 66% of Gen Z consumers say campaigns launching as early as August make them more likely to buy, compared to 49% of consumers overall.

Tariffs and price pressure are reshaping purchase patterns

Many consumers see shopping earlier as a way to get ahead of rising prices. More than a third (36%) say they’re starting their holiday shopping earlier specifically to avoid tariff-related price increases. Another 27% aren’t shopping earlier yet but are concerned about prices.

In total, 63% of holiday shoppers are thinking about the impact of higher prices.

Those concerns are also affecting how much consumers plan to spend. More than half (56%) expect to reduce their holiday spending this year because of economic conditions like tariffs and the cost of living. Only 30% say they don’t plan to cut back.

Price sensitivity doesn’t mean every brand needs to compete on having the lowest price. Shoppers may be looking more closely at what they get for their money, so holiday content should make value clear. Highlight product quality, versatility or other details that make a purchase feel worthwhile.

Discounts can also tip the scales: Promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top purchase driver, cited by 30% of consumers. Lastly, brands with products at multiple price points can also organize gift recommendations by budget, making it easier for shoppers to find options that work for them.

For example, last holiday season, REI shared a roundup of expert picks under $50 on Instagram, with a CTA to check out their larger holiday gift guide.

Consumers are discovering gifts on social this year

Social media now rivals in-store shopping for holiday gift discovery. This year, 46% of consumers say they’ll turn to social for gift ideas and product discovery—the same percentage who plan to browse physical stores.

Where consumers turn for holiday gift ideas:

  • Social media: 46%
  • Physical stores: 46%
  • Recommendations from friends and family: 34%
  • TV: 31%
  • Review sites: 23%
  • AI chatbots: 15%

And social’s influence is still growing. Compared to the 2025 holiday season, 28% of consumers plan to use social more to find gifts this year, while another 50% expect their usage to stay about the same.

That creates an opportunity to reach shoppers before they know exactly what they want to buy.

Think about how easily someone encountering your brand for the first time can understand what you sell, who your products are for and why they’re worth considering. Content organized around recipients, interests, occasions or price points can make that discovery process easier and give shoppers a reason to explore your products further.

Bookshop.org, for example, used Instagram to promote its 2025 holiday gift guide, which curated hundreds of recommendations for different types of readers and paired them with a limited-time discount.

What drives a purchase on social?

Discovery is only the first step. Once shoppers find a product on social, the content surrounding it can influence whether they buy.

According to the Q3 2026 pulse survey, promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top social-specific purchase trigger at 30%, followed closely by brand posts showing products in action at 28%. Original holiday content from brands influences 26% of consumers, while 22% point to content from non-influencer users.

articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • PR budgets could double by 2027 as brands adapt to AI-powered search.
  • AI systems increasingly rely on authoritative third-party sources when generating answers and recommendations.
  • Digital PR can help brands build visibility and credibility beyond their own websites.

  • Brands should connect digital PR with SEO and AI visibility rather than treating them as separate strategies.

For years, public relations and SEO have operated in neighboring but often separate parts of the marketing organization. AI search is beginning to change that relationship.

As AI systems become a larger part of how people discover companies, products, and services, the sources those systems rely on are becoming increasingly important. Third-party coverage from trusted publications can provide information that helps establish a brand’s credibility and authority.
That shift is changing how organizations think about digital PR.
New industry projections suggest PR budgets could double by 2027 as brands respond to the growing importance of AI-powered search. The underlying reason is straightforward: brands need to be visible in the places AI systems use to understand and evaluate them.
For marketers, that makes earned media more than a traditional awareness channel. Consistent third-party coverage can contribute to a brand’s broader search presence while strengthening the information available about it across the web.

Why AI Search Is Increasing the Value of Digital PR

AI search changes how people encounter information. Instead of receiving a list of links and deciding which ones to visit, users can receive a synthesized answer based on information gathered from multiple sources.

That creates a new role for third-party coverage.

Source

AI Systems Rely on Trusted Sources

AI systems need information they can retrieve and use when generating answers.

A company’s own website is an important source, but it isn’t the only one. News publications, industry websites, reviews, research organizations, and other third-party sources can provide additional context about a brand. Academic databases are a great example.

This is where earned media becomes valuable.

A company that is consistently mentioned by credible publications creates a broader information footprint than one that relies primarily on its own website. Those mentions can help reinforce what the company does, who its experts are, and where it has authority.

That doesn’t guarantee an AI system will cite any particular article. It does create more opportunities for a brand’s information to exist within the sources AI systems may encounter.

Third-Party Coverage Can Build Brand Authority

Authority is difficult to establish through a single piece of coverage.

One major publication can create awareness, but its effect can fade. A sustained presence across relevant publications creates a different type of signal.

Repeated coverage can reinforce the same core facts about a business across multiple sources. Over time, this can contribute to stronger brand recognition and a clearer understanding of the company’s expertise.

For AI visibility, that consistency matters because AI systems are constantly processing information from across the web.

Why One Media Win Isn’t Enough

The temptation in PR has often been to measure success by the biggest placement a campaign can generate. A marquee publication can certainly be valuable, but it shouldn’t be the only objective.

Credibility Compounds Over Time

A single article can introduce a company to a new audience. An ongoing stream of relevant coverage can keep reinforcing the brand.

articles.title: What’s Making AI Impact Difficult to Measure for Marketers?
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Brands recommended by ChatGPT were 2.5x more likely to receive a website visit within seven days, according to Similarweb research.
  • Most AI-influenced visits did not arrive through an identifiable AI referral.
  • More than half of AI-influenced visits arrived through search, meaning the AI influence can look like ordinary organic traffic in analytics.
  • Last-click attribution can therefore underestimate the role AI plays in brand discovery and consideration.
  • Marketers need broader measurement frameworks that account for AI’s influence across the customer journey.

AI search is becoming an increasingly important way for consumers to discover brands. But measuring its impact is proving much harder than measuring a traditional referral.

A user might ask ChatGPT for a product recommendation, see a brand mentioned, and then search for that brand on Google several days later. Analytics will record the eventual visit, but it may have no way of knowing that an AI recommendation helped start the journey.

New research from Similarweb highlights the scale of this measurement gap. Brands recommended by ChatGPT were 2.5x more likely to receive a website visit within the following seven days, even when there was no direct referral from the AI platform.

The finding suggests that AI visibility can influence traffic without appearing as AI traffic in a standard analytics report.

For marketers, that’s an important distinction. If AI is influencing customers before they reach a website, measuring only the final click can make the channel look less valuable than it actually is.

What Similarweb Found About AI’s Downstream Impact

Similarweb’s research tracked real user journeys to understand what happens after a brand is recommended in ChatGPT.

Source

AI Recommendations Can Lead to More Website Visits</h3>

Similarweb followed users who asked ChatGPT an industry-related question and received a specific brand recommendation. It then tracked their behavior over the following seven days.

Across finance, travel, and beauty, users who received an AI recommendation for a brand were 2.5x more likely to visit that brand’s website than users who received a recommendation for a competing brand.

The research focused on users who had not previously visited the recommended brand and had not already mentioned that brand in their prompt. This helped Similarweb measure the downstream effect of a recommendation rather than simply tracking people who already knew about a company.

The result provides a useful signal for marketers investing in AI visibility. Being mentioned in an AI answer can influence what consumers do afterward, even when the AI platform doesn’t send the eventual website visit.

Most of the Traffic Doesn’t Look Like AI Traffic

This is where traditional measurement becomes complicated.

Similarweb found that 55.9% of AI-influenced visits arrived through search, compared with 40.4% of visits without AI influence.

In practice, that means a user could see a brand recommendation in ChatGPT, remember the name, and later search for it on Google.

That visit would likely be attributed to organic search.

The AI interaction that helped create the interest would receive no credit.

This is the core AI attribution problem. The measurable traffic is real, but the original source of influence can disappear somewhere between discovery and conversion.

Source

Why Last-Click Attribution Misses AI’s Influence

Last-click attribution works reasonably well when a customer journey is relatively direct. But discovery through AI can introduce additional steps that aren’t captured by traditional referral reporting.

The AI Interaction Happens Before the Measurable Visit

Consider a simple journey.

A consumer asks an AI platform which software tools are best for their business. The platform recommends a brand. The consumer doesn’t click a link. Instead, they continue researching, then return to Google two days later and search for the brand by name.

From an analytics perspective, the final visit may look like a branded organic search.

From the customer’s perspective, however, the journey started with AI.

In 2009, by issuing a call to arms to “make the web faster”, Google set out on a mission to try and persuade website owners to make their sites load more quickly.

In order to entice website owners into actually caring about this, in 2010 Google announced that site speed would become a factor in its desktop (non-mobile) search engine ranking algorithms. This meant that sites that loaded quickly would have an SEO advantage over other websites.

Six years later, in 2015, Google announced that the number of searches performed on mobile exceeded those performed on desktop computers. That percentage continues to increase. The latest published statistic says that, as of 2019, 61% of searches performed on Google were from mobile devices.

Mobile’s now-dominant role in search led Google to develop its “Accelerated Mobile Pages” (AMP) project. This initiative is aimed at encouraging website owners to create what is essentially another mobile theme, on top of their responsive mobile theme, that complies with a very strict set of development and performance guidelines.

Although many site owners and SEOs complain about having to tend to page speed and AMP on top of the other 200+ ranking factors that already give them headaches, page speed is indeed a worthy effort for site owners to focus on. In 2017, Google conducted a study where the results very much justified their focus on making the web faster. They found that “As page load time goes from one second to 10 seconds, the probability of a mobile site visitor bouncing increases 123%.”
articles.description: Winning the page speed race requires the same things as winning a car race: making sure that your vehicle is as lightweight as possible, as powerful as possible, and that you navigate the racetrack as efficiently as possible.

Responsive search ads are very flexible ads that automatically adapt to show the right message to the right customer. You enter multiple headlines and descriptions when creating the ad. According to Google, advertisers who use responsive search ads in their ad groups can achieve an increase of up to 10% more clicks and conversions as compared to standard text ads.

Mobile-friendly: They are very flexible and can adapt to fit devices of different widths. Most online searches are made on mobile devices. These ads can adapt to show fewer headlines and descriptions on mobile devices.
